title: Why has Elemental been so poorly received?

commenti.body:
I think visually, it just feels bland and like something we've seen before. I haven't seen it and noone in the house has asked to see it, which is strange considering we have 3 children under age 8 in the house. I'm fan of animation of all types, including past Disney releases, but to me going in, it feels like a generic Inside Out meets Zootopia, which gives me less impetus to watch it as well.   


You can look back at other films starring inanimate objects, and I think you need a really strong plot and performances to make it work (Inside Out) to make that emotional connection. I freaking love Bing Bong as a character, and always will. Whereas even with a big one from my childhoold Brave Little Toaster, its just not memorable because I don't experience things as an inanimate object, or as the concept of fire, or sadness.  


Films like these need a human element to ground and help map things for the human audience. Is that missing from Elemental? Because I care about people and then animals, and the other life and creations of our earth, but I don't care how wind, fire, or water are doing.
[removed]

They don't explore the city enough. They go to a few places, you live in the world a little bit, and then there's a formulaic, weak climax with no complex themes other than basically 'bigot bad'. The movie could've been big, but it opted to feel small. I enjoyed it, I liked the characters, and it looked amazing, but it's no more than a 7.5/10 for me.

Well the story focuses on Ember and her family’s experience as immigrants, and how the city isn’t built for newcomers - in fact, it’s almost actively built against them. And then it focuses on the love story between her and Wade, in essentially a romcom formula. It didn’t ever seem to me like it was supposed to be a vast story exploring the whole city or the world; it seemed very clearly focused to me
If you haven’t seen it why are you contributing to this discussion?
You are asking why is it being poorly received, and I listed reasons? You think that visual presentation doesn't play a part?

I haven't seen it, maybe it's great, but I can tell you why I had no desire to watch it and maybe it'll help answer your question anyway?

There was a meme a while ago about Pixar up until Inside Out that went something like this:

1. What if toys had feelings?
2. What if bugs had feelings?
3. What if monsters had feelings?
4. What if fish has feelings?
5. What if cars had feelings?
6. What if FEELINGS had feelings??

I think when I look at Elemental, I get the sense of people in a writers room saying "I dunno, the elements? What if they had feelings?"

I just think conceptually it sounds like throwing shit at the wall and seeing if it sticks. The ancient elements aren't really something people think about or interact with often, and not something that makes sense to put a face on. I think it's just hard to connect with?

But, like I say, I didn't see it and even the worst Pixar films manage to draw a tear out of my eye. I don't doubt it's good and I'm glad you enjoyed it! I just couldn't get excited about it, personally.

This is a valid perspective answering the OP's question from an outsider's perspective as to why they haven't seen it. IE part of the "poorly received" crowd. I fall in the same camp. Don't get so defensive, OP.

Oh man I had a rough time watching this. I didn't like the character design or art style at all. Its pretty different sure, but theres something really unappealing and ugly about it. And its really just typical Pixar not doing anything new. Inanimate objects dealing with a topical issue (immigration & racism) in a way that doesn't feel totally sincere or fleshed out. Didn't find the characters interesting & the center romance has no chemistry or believability. The water guy in particular was also super annoying.

It’s too grownup for children and too childish for grownups. 

Because the crying game. 

Because it lacks subtlety to make it interesting and also lacks whimsy to make it fun. 

The main antagonist is beurocracy and as such it’s engaging as such. 

It comes of as bland and safe, lacking any real ambition or joy.

I don’t hate it, but just didn’t love it. It’s a solid 7/10 for me which would be a lower grade for a Pixar movie (even tho they have been on that track for a while now.)

I really like the visual. I like the city itself but I do wish we get to see more. Her trouble of wanting to make her own path while wanting to pass on her immigrant parents tradition hit too close to home for me. 

I just feels like there’s one too many storyline to the movie. I think the romance and the family story itself could be strong enough if the movie focuses on that, but the dam leak feels like it’s too just feels like a really leads to nowhere but only to add a physical threat to the third act. In the beginning it suggest a wider social conspiracy but no, the city officials just didn’t notice that and in fact, acted really quick, but also, the solution is not good enough and it still just broke. So it doesn’t work as a metaphor for the wider message of the movie. It’s clunky in the story itself. And the third act still feel anticlimactic. It just feels like a water down version of Zootopia.

Yea I think my main visual issue was how odd the characters looked in context of the environment, which I think was aesthetically pleasing. I felt like the fire people could've looked fine in a different art style. Water people looked rough. Very much not a fan of most of the humor either, I thought a lot of jokes were just hard to sit through.

You're totally right. For me it's just too focused. I guess I just want more. The romantic stuff in movies almost never moves me because it's all fake. What really moves me is intelligent writing, dialogue, character growth, and world building. Some movie romantic relationships that I would say were a bit more meaningful and complex to me would be Punch Drunk Love, Licorice Pizza, Her, Lost in Translation, Enemy, even Vengeance or Champions.

my general feeling on it was while it had a lot of heart, the metaphor was ultimately what let it down. on the one hand i liked how the physical differences of the elements stood in for affective dissonances often felt between people of different races, but on the other i felt that it was odd the way it portrayed what is metaphorically an interracial relationship as something so novel and groundbreaking in 2023. i just couldn't help but wonder why the writers felt it was necessary to tell kids that yes, you can date or be friends with people of other races. while segregation is certainly still a problem in many cities today, its insistence on dividing the elements up so thoroughly ("elements can't mix") seemed to me oddly out of sync with reality in a way i felt was ultimately detrimental to its messaging

I thought it was ok(6/10). Some good messages and the romance is cute but the plot is pretty boring(they’re fixing a dam). I also think the move does a terrible job actually building its world that feels lived in or makes sense in anyway. Also what’s the point of having a four elements if there’s barely any use of the other two (why not just make it Fire and Water).
[removed]

There's a short film called Good Chemistry where the director (a 1st gen Korean immigrant) explains how he got the idea for the film when he looked at the periodic table and imagined it as an apartment complex where all of the elements were forced to live on top of each other. Which is a pretty intriguing concept IMO, but it never really materializes in the execution. Ember makes multiple comments about how city "isn't built with fire people in mind," but we don't really see how this manifests structurally other than the occasional splash of water. By focusing so tightly on her and Wade's relationship and respective upbringings, the world-building suffers. 

I will say that I think this film is a beautiful encapsulation of the immigrant experience and the social pressures unique to (in my experience) Asian-American children. I also think that some of the representation of bigotry is nuanced (like how the guy who changes her parents' names at the quasi-Ellis Island entrance is trying to be helpful and accommodating, just a little ignorant and ostensibly overworked). I just wish we'd gotten to spend more time in Elemental City itself and understand how the threat of a villainous bureaucracy really impacts these characters lives. As it stands, the stakes of the conflict remain pretty tame and narrow.

I also didn’t go see the film, and I think this is one of the reasons why. The trailer also made me feel like I’d already seen everything there is to see.

Elements are stereotypes.
Romeo and Juliet story.
Everyone turns into a slightly better person by welcoming difference into their lives, blabla.

If that’s not what the movie is, cool. But that’s what the marketing told me it was so eh.
That's the movie to a T

TBH, I just don't the story was that compelling. I enjoyed Encanto, Turning Red, EEAO all more than this. I think I'm getting fatigued by these kinds of immigrant stories, but I also think the ones I've listed had stronger narratives.

I simply did not care about Wade and Ember. I also did not care about Ember's "conflict" with her dad. I honestly cared the most about Ember's dad I think.

Also using Elements as an allegory for race is as messy as using predators and prey a la Zootopia. There are very convincing reasons why miscegenation is not a thing in Elemental (eg. potential death), which was weirdly a point they make in the film?

Also Asian American here. Curious to see what you read as being unique to Asian American children. TBH, my reading of it was specific to 2nd generation Asian Americans and not Asian Americans as a whole and TBH could be related more to the "child of immigrant" experience (eg. filial piety) more so than the shared Asian American experience (ie. racism)

I didn’t hate it. It was pretty middle of the road. The world for me was poorly fleshed out, especially compared to Zootopia, which also handled the topic of racism in an interesting way with a character who is the subject of targeted racism her whole life and then when she gets recognition, the first thing she does is be racist right back to another group. The mystery was the framing device for a story of tolerance.

Elemental is more blunt in its messaging. What you see is what you get. Another Romeo and Juliet-esq film that says racism bad.

Yeah sorry for not clarifying: I meant 2nd gen children, specifically the pressure to follow the life and career path expected of you by your parents as unspoken "payback" for the immense sacrifices they made in order to create a life in America. I know that's a very common feeling among people of various background and ethnicities.

Yeah I watched about half an hour and thought it was boring and cliche, and pretty much completely predictable in a way Pixar usually avoids. I think it's the only Pixar movie yet I've started but didn't finish, though some like Cars 2 I skipped.

i get what you mean about the characters looking odd in the environment. i felt the water people could've been done better. also, some of the humor fell flat for me. i think the concept of the elements having feelings is a bit of a stretch, but i'm glad you enjoyed it!

I enjoyed Elemental just as much as OP, because even though the concept itself feels a bit gimmicky, I thought it comes out as a creative and fun romcom, which was the movie's main intention after all.

I think people tend to be harsh on Pixar because they hold the studio at a very high standard. However, some of their recent movies that became critical darlings, such as Coco and Soul, could be accused of the same faults here - those don't explore the death realm and the afterlife world too much either, and eventually I get the feeling that they were seen as "serious Pixar" because of their themes. Yet those themes were somewhat repetitive. Pixar was too obsessed with death for quite some time. It's nice to get a lighthearted movie as a change.

OP, I agree. I thought “Elemental” was a real treat: a gorgeously animated romcom (a first for the studio!) that sets its “will-they-won’t-they” story in a highly inventive world. While the narrative is simple and predictable, you can see how much creativity was put into the execution. 

Checking the response from critics afterwards, I was also surprised to find mostly lukewarm reviews stemming from the same basic argument: “it’s fine, but it’s not up to Pixar’s best”. I’m sure that, by “Pixar’s best”, they’re referring to the early instant classics like “Toy Story”, “Finding Nemo”, “Ratatouille” or “Up”. And while Pixar DID had an impeccable record for the first 15-somewhat-years of its history in producing feature-length animations, I think it’s unfair to expect every release should be an undeniable masterpiece. 

Do you remember “Kung Fu Panda” or “How to Train Your Dragon” being compared (favorably or unfavorably) to “Shrek”? Me neither. All these movies came from the same studio, were all hugely successful and inspired sequels and spin-offs of their own. Yet they were all recognized by their individual qualities at the time of their release. In fact, since DreamWorks Animation had a somewhat uneven track record, constantly alternating between hits and misses, it was easy to spot a truly good movie when it came along (like Panda, like Dragon), even if they didn’t initially seem like a game-changing “all-timer”. 

Pixar, coming from a string of early hits, will always be held at a higher stander. And it’s true that, since it was acquired by Disney, Pixar delved deep into prequels and sequels and spin-offs of its early successes, to different results. The movies that are mostly praised by critics are originals, yet only the originals that are perceived as “important”, the ones that handle more serious, grown-up topics. For Pixar, the theme of death has been a good-luck charm: “Coco” and “Soul” were lauded as instant classics, but years later, those aren’t conversation starters like old Pixar. 

“Elemental”, on the other hand, had a strong word of mouth and a respectful box-office after struggling in the opening weekend. That means audiences connected to the movie, and its quality as a lighthearted, fun romcom was not missed on its viewers.

I'd argue Coco is only so fondly remembered because of the the colors and the culture. I actually think it's one of the worst Pixar movies for the reason you mentioned. The entire third act is throwaway. Soul is an amazing film, but you're totally right, the day feels so short. I also had an issue with 23's voice actor coming out of Joe Gardner's mouth, very poor choice. I'd still argue that Soul brings a lot more to the table than Elemental.

The problem isn't that elemental isn't enough, it's that Elements starts to get really interesting, but then it just suddenly ends. And also that in terms of character writing and world building, the execution is so high, yet it opts for a deflating ending, in a location we've already seen 50 times.

Here's what I think! Coco packs a huge emotional punch with the Remember Me song, but the movie itself was too predictable to my taste (I saw the twist coming in the first 30 minutes), and the worldbuilding itself was basically generic. 

Soul was a HUGE letdown to me. The entire afterlife realm is visually unimaginative, mostly due to the basic character design, and the concepts they try to execute aren’t well established over the narrative. Inside Out was also a high-concept movie, but it was able to set the scene from the intro alone: how emotions work, how core memories build islands of personality and so on. In Soul, we’re still learning basic concepts of this world building as the story progresses. It also resorts to an animation gimmick to have a black lead character is deprived of its identity for most of the movie. The first black Disney princess spends most of “The Princess and the Frog” turned into a green frog. Just like Spies in Disguise turns Will Smith into a pigeon. The black lead in Soul is seen mostly as a blue spirit or as Tina Fey, a white woman, inhabiting his body. Tina Fey’s experiences while roaming the Earth for one day makes him finally understand the meaning of life. Tina Fey plays a “soul” that has no real understanding of the human experience, and her naivety is portrayed as insightful. 

Coco’s version of the Death realm was like a colorful slum. The characters meet Frida Kahlo, because she’s the most recognizable Mexican icon that came to mind, I guess? Soul’s afterlife world is minimalistic as heck, visual-wise. Elementals has more inventiveness and visual gags than Coco and Soul combined. If we watch the movie already aware of its intentions – this is a fantasy romcom -, we won’t expect it to “get good”, because the movie's simplistic storytelling can be interesting on its own.

i get where you're coming from, but i actually loved how the characters were designed to fit the environment. the humor worked for me too, felt genuine. i think the concept of giving feelings to the elements was a fresh take and made the story more relatable. glad you enjoyed it!
